claim: Mucosal bacterial infections account for over 42 million outpatient visits annually in the United States.
source: Mucosal bacterial infections are very common, accounting for over 42 million outpatient visits and a majority of the 270 million outpatient antibiotic prescriptions in the United States annually (Armstrong and Pinner, 1999; May et al., 2014; Outpatient antibiotic prescriptions, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Armstrong and Pinner, 1999; May et al., 2014; Outpatient antibiotic prescriptions, 2011

claim: Mucosal bacterial infections account for a majority of the 270 million outpatient antibiotic prescriptions in the United States annually.
source: Mucosal bacterial infections are very common, accounting for over 42 million outpatient visits and a majority of the 270 million outpatient antibiotic prescriptions in the United States annually (Armstrong and Pinner, 1999; May et al., 2014; Outpatient antibiotic prescriptions, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Armstrong and Pinner, 1999; May et al., 2014; Outpatient antibiotic prescriptions, 2011

claim: Urinary tract infections lead to over $2 billion in direct and indirect costs annually in the United States.
source: Of these, respiratory and urinary tract infections (UTI) can be highly recurrent, the latter leading to over $2 billion in direct and indirect costs annually in the United States (Foxman, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Foxman, 2010

claim: Over 80% of community-acquired UTI are caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC).
source: Over 80% of community-acquired UTI are caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) (Gupta and Bhadelia, 2014; Ronald, 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gupta and Bhadelia, 2014; Ronald, 2003

claim: The vast majority of UPEC infections involve the lower urinary tract and specifically the urinary bladder, causing cystitis.
source: the vast majority of these infections involve the lower urinary tract and specifically the urinary bladder, causing cystitis (bladder infection).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Over 60% of women will experience at least one UTI during their lifetime.
source: Women are disproportionately affected: over 60% of women will experience at least one UTI during their lifetime (Foxman et al., 2000a)
evidence: Supported by citation to Foxman et al., 2000a

claim: 20–30% of women who experience a UTI will experience a recurrence within 6 months.
source: of these women, 20–30% will experience a recurrence (rUTI) within 6 months (Foxman et al., 2000b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Foxman et al., 2000b

claim: Some individuals with recurrent UTI resort to taking daily suppressive antibiotic therapy to prevent further recurrence.
source: Some individuals experience recurrent UTI to such a high degree that they resort to taking daily suppressive antibiotic therapy to prevent further recurrence (Ikäheimo et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ikäheimo et al., 1996

claim: In sexually active young women, a history of two or more UTIs is one of the single biggest independent risk factors for developing an acute UTI.
source: In sexually active young women, one of the single biggest independent risk factors for developing an acute UTI is a history of two or more UTIs (Hooton et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hooton et al., 1996

claim: For some women, UTI infections resolve spontaneously within a few days, while others may develop persistent bladder infections lasting for weeks.
source: Furthermore, placebo studies of UTI patients show that the natural course of infection and symptoms can vary greatly: for some women, infections resolve spontaneously within a few days, while others may develop persistent bladder infections lasting for weeks (Ferry et al., 2004; Christiaens et al., 2002; Mabeck, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferry et al., 2004; Christiaens et al., 2002; Mabeck, 1972

claim: Disease history may impact the nature of the future interaction of UPEC with the urinary tract mucosa of patients in a way that alters susceptibility to symptomatic rUTI.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that disease history may impact the nature of the future interaction of UPEC with the urinary tract mucosa of patients in a way that alters susceptibility to symptomatic rUTI.
evidence: Inferred from cited clinical data on UTI variability and recurrence patterns

claim: In C3H/HeN mice, a dichotomy of self-resolving vs. chronic infection occurs after experimental UPEC infection in an infectious dose-dependent manner.
source: In C3H/HeN mice, a dichotomy of self-resolving vs. chronic infection, similar to the natural course of UTI in women, occurs after experimental UPEC infection in an infectious dose-dependent manner (Hannan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hannan et al., 2010

claim: Mice that spontaneously resolve the initial infection are highly resistant to rUTI upon challenge.
source: Strikingly, the outcome of the initial infection polarizes future susceptibility to rUTI: mice that spontaneously resolve the initial infection are highly resistant to rUTI upon challenge, whereas those that develop an initial chronic infection (persistent high-titer bladder bacterial colonization and bladder mucosal inflammation) lasting two weeks or longer prior to antibiotic therapy are highly sensitive to rUTI (O'Brien et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Brien et al., 2015

claim: Mice that develop an initial chronic infection lasting two weeks or longer prior to antibiotic therapy are highly sensitive to rUTI.
source: Strikingly, the outcome of the initial infection polarizes future susceptibility to rUTI: mice that spontaneously resolve the initial infection are highly resistant to rUTI upon challenge, whereas those that develop an initial chronic infection (persistent high-titer bladder bacterial colonization and bladder mucosal inflammation) lasting two weeks or longer prior to antibiotic therapy are highly sensitive to rUTI (O'Brien et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Brien et al., 2015

claim: At 24 hours post-inoculation, elevated serum cytokines (IL-5, IL-6, G-CSF, CXCL1), severe bladder inflammation with mucosal wounding, and pyuria are the hallmarks of checkpoint activation indicating severe acute UTI that predisposes to chronic infection.
source: Specifically, at 24 hours post-inoculation (hpi), elevated serum cytokines (IL-5, IL-6, G-CSF, CXCL1), severe bladder inflammation with mucosal wounding, and pyuria (neutrophils in urine) are the hallmarks of checkpoint activation, which indicates severe acute UTI that predisposes to chronic infection.
evidence: Stated as established finding from prior work in this model system

claim: Robust cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression by bladder epithelial cells at 24 hpi promotes neutrophil transmigration through the urothelium, causing mucosal damage and ultimately the development of chronic cystitis.
source: In mice that trigger the checkpoint, robust cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) expression by bladder epithelial (urothelial) cells at 24 hpi promotes neutrophil transmigration through the urothelium, causing mucosal damage and ultimately the development of chronic cystitis (Hannan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hannan et al., 2014

claim: If chronic cystitis is permitted to go on for two or more weeks prior to antibiotic therapy, affected mice become highly susceptible to developing severe rUTI upon subsequent challenge in a COX-2 dependent manner.
source: If chronic cystitis is permitted to go on for two or more weeks prior to antibiotic therapy, affected mice then become highly susceptible to developing severe rUTI upon subsequent challenge in a COX-2 dependent manner (Hannan et al., 2010; Hannan et al., 2014; O'Brien et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hannan et al., 2010; Hannan et al., 2014; O'Brien et al., 2016

claim: C57BL/6J mice can be induced to develop chronic cystitis by repeated bacterial inoculation.
source: C57BL/6J mice, though inherently resistant to chronic cystitis upon a single bladder inoculation of UPEC, can be induced to develop chronic cystitis by repeated bacterial inoculation (Hannan et al., 2010; Schwartz et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hannan et al., 2010; Schwartz et al., 2015

claim: C57BL/6J mice with a history of chronic infection become susceptible to severe rUTI upon challenge, similar to C3H/HeN mice.
source: those with a history of chronic infection become susceptible to severe rUTI upon challenge, similar to C3H/HeN mice, demonstrating that acquired factors related to a prior chronic infection can overcome genetic resistance (O'Brien et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Brien et al., 2016

claim: Acquired factors related to a prior chronic infection can overcome genetic resistance to severe rUTI.
source: those with a history of chronic infection become susceptible to severe rUTI upon challenge, similar to C3H/HeN mice, demonstrating that acquired factors related to a prior chronic infection can overcome genetic resistance (O'Brien et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Brien et al., 2016 and inference from experimental results

claim: Serum cytokine biomarkers associated with more robust granulocytic responses are predictive of susceptibility to rUTI in women.
source: Translating these findings to humans, we found that serum cytokine biomarkers associated with more robust granulocytic responses, similar to those associated with the development of chronic cystitis in naive mice, were also predictive of susceptibility to rUTI in women (Hannan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hannan et al., 2014

claim: The diverging susceptibilities of mice to rUTI as a consequence of the outcome of a prior infection are due in part to bladder remodeling that alters the pathophysiology of acute cystitis upon the second infection.
source: The diverging susceptibilities of mice to rUTI as a consequence of the outcome of a prior infection were found to be due in part to bladder remodeling that alters the pathophysiology of acute cystitis upon the second infection (Hannan et al., 2014; O'Brien et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hannan et al., 2014; O'Brien et al., 2016

claim: A prior bladder infection resulted in an earlier onset of TNFα-mediated bladder inflammation upon subsequent bacterial challenge, relative to age-matched naive mice.
source: We investigated this question in a mouse model of recurrent urinary tract infection and found that a prior bladder infection resulted in an earlier onset of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFɑ)-mediated bladder inflammation upon subsequent bacterial challenge, relative to age-matched naive mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The duration of TNFα signaling activation differed according to whether the first infection was chronic (Sensitized) or self-limiting (Resolved).
source: However, the duration of TNFɑ signaling activation differed according to whether the first infection was chronic (Sensitized) or self-limiting (Resolved).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Transient early-phase TNFα signaling in Resolved mice promoted clearance of bladder-colonizing bacteria via rapid recruitment of neutrophils and subsequent exfoliation of infected bladder cells.
source: TNFɑ depletion studies revealed that transient early-phase TNFɑ signaling in Resolved mice promoted clearance of bladder-colonizing bacteria via rapid recruitment of neutrophils and subsequent exfoliation of infected bladder cells.
evidence: Supported by TNFα depletion experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Sustained TNFα signaling in Sensitized mice prolonged damaging inflammation, worsening infection.
source: In contrast, sustained TNFɑ signaling in Sensitized mice prolonged damaging inflammation, worsening infection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The majority of Resolved and Sensitized mice had severe bladder inflammation at 6 hpi with median bladder histopathology scores of 5 for each group.
source: Whereas the majority of Resolved and Sensitized mice had severe bladder inflammation (median bladder histopathology scores of 5 for each group) at 6 hpi, none of the Adult Naive mice had severe bladder inflammation (median histopathology score of 2.5).
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 1B-C

claim: None of the Adult Naive mice had severe bladder inflammation at 6 hpi with a median histopathology score of 2.5.
source: Whereas the majority of Resolved and Sensitized mice had severe bladder inflammation (median bladder histopathology scores of 5 for each group) at 6 hpi, none of the Adult Naive mice had severe bladder inflammation (median histopathology score of 2.5).
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 1B-C

claim: By 24 hpi, the severity of bladder inflammation had waned significantly in Resolved mice with a median bladder histopathology score of 1.
source: By 24 hpi, the severity of bladder inflammation had waned significantly in Resolved mice and trended lower in Sensitized mice (median bladder histopathology scores of 1 and 2, respectively), but had increased in Adult Naive mice, though not to a severe level in most individuals, with a median bladder histopathology score of 3.5.
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 1B-C

claim: By 24 hpi, bladder inflammation trended lower in Sensitized mice with a median bladder histopathology score of 2.
source: By 24 hpi, the severity of bladder inflammation had waned significantly in Resolved mice and trended lower in Sensitized mice (median bladder histopathology scores of 1 and 2, respectively), but had increased in Adult Naive mice, though not to a severe level in most individuals, with a median bladder histopathology score of 3.5.
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 1B-C

claim: By 24 hpi, bladder inflammation had increased in Adult Naive mice with a median bladder histopathology score of 3.5.
source: By 24 hpi, the severity of bladder inflammation had waned significantly in Resolved mice and trended lower in Sensitized mice (median bladder histopathology scores of 1 and 2, respectively), but had increased in Adult Naive mice, though not to a severe level in most individuals, with a median bladder histopathology score of 3.5.
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 1B-C

claim: Significantly lower bladder bacterial titers were observed at 6 hpi in mice with a history of UTI relative to Adult Naive mice.
source: Consistent with previous work using a 107 cfu challenge (O'Brien et al., 2016), we observed significantly lower titers at 6 hpi in mice with a history of UTI relative to Adult Naive mice (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 2A and citation to O'Brien et al., 2016

claim: At 24 hpi, a bimodal distribution of bladder bacterial burdens was observed in mice with a previous history of UTI.
source: At 24 hpi, a bimodal distribution of bladder bacterial burdens was observed in mice with a previous history of UTI, with 11 of 14 Sensitized mice experiencing a bloom of UPEC to levels between 105 and 108 cfu/bladder.
evidence: Supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 11 of 14 Sensitized mice experienced a bloom of UPEC to levels between 10^5 and 10^8 cfu/bladder at 24 hpi.
source: At 24 hpi, a bimodal distribution of bladder bacterial burdens was observed in mice with a previous history of UTI, with 11 of 14 Sensitized mice experiencing a bloom of UPEC to levels between 105 and 108 cfu/bladder.
evidence: Supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The median bacterial burden in Sensitized mice increased from 3.2 × 10^4 at 6 hpi to 8.6 × 10^5 cfu/bladder at 24 hpi.
source: These titers are similar to or higher than those seen in Adult Naive mice, with an increase in overall median bacterial burden from 3.2 × 104 at 6 hpi to 8.6 × 105 cfu/bladder at 24 hpi.
evidence: Supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The median bacterial burden in Resolved mice decreased from 1.7 × 10^5 at 6 hpi to 1.6 × 10^4 cfu/bladder at 24 hpi.
source: In contrast, the median bacterial burden in Resolved mice decreased from 1.7 × 105 at 6 hpi to 1.6 × 104 cfu/bladder at 24 hpi, though 6 of 17 mice had high bacterial burdens above 105 cfu/bladder at 24 hpi (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 2A

claim: 6 of 17 Resolved mice had high bacterial burdens above 10^5 cfu/bladder at 24 hpi.
source: In contrast, the median bacterial burden in Resolved mice decreased from 1.7 × 105 at 6 hpi to 1.6 × 104 cfu/bladder at 24 hpi, though 6 of 17 mice had high bacterial burdens above 105 cfu/bladder at 24 hpi (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Only one of 25 Resolved mice infected with 10^8 cfu UTI89 developed chronic infection lasting four weeks.
source: However, this subset of Resolved mice with higher bladder titers at 24 hpi did not reflect a propensity for chronic infection, as only one of 25 Resolved mice infected with 108 cfu UTI89 developed chronic infection lasting four weeks, levels similar to those seen in 'resistant' C57BL/6J mice (Hannan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Hannan et al., 2010

claim: The pattern of bladder edema mirrored the patterns of bladder inflammation observed by histopathology.
source: The pattern of bladder edema as indicated by the weights of these bladders mirrored the patterns of bladder inflammation observed by histopathology (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by bladder weight data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Previously infected mice (Resolved or Sensitized) had significantly increased bladder weights at 6 hpi relative to mock-infected mice with the same infection history.
source: Most notably, previously infected mice, whether Resolved or Sensitized, had significantly increased bladder weights at 6 hpi (relative to mock-infected mice with the same infection history) that by 24 hpi had decreased significantly in Resolved mice but remained elevated in Sensitized mice.
evidence: Supported by bladder weight data shown in Figure 2B

claim: By 24 hpi, bladder weights had decreased significantly in Resolved mice but remained elevated in Sensitized mice.
source: Most notably, previously infected mice, whether Resolved or Sensitized, had significantly increased bladder weights at 6 hpi (relative to mock-infected mice with the same infection history) that by 24 hpi had decreased significantly in Resolved mice but remained elevated in Sensitized mice.
evidence: Supported by bladder weight data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Bladder weights in Adult Naive mice were not significantly increased until 24 hpi.
source: Bladder weights in Adult Naive mice were not significantly increased until 24 hpi.
evidence: Supported by bladder weight data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Bladder levels of IL-6, CXCL1, and CCL2 were sharply increased at 6 hpi in previously infected mice relative to Adult Naive mice.
source: Bladder levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, CXCL1, and CCL2 followed similar patterns, with sharply increased levels at 6 hpi in previously infected mice relative to Adult Naive mice and waning of these levels by 24 hpi in Resolved, but not in Sensitized, mice.
evidence: Supported by cytokine data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Bladder levels of IL-6, CXCL1, and CCL2 waned by 24 hpi in Resolved, but not in Sensitized, mice.
source: Bladder levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, CXCL1, and CCL2 followed similar patterns, with sharply increased levels at 6 hpi in previously infected mice relative to Adult Naive mice and waning of these levels by 24 hpi in Resolved, but not in Sensitized, mice.
evidence: Supported by cytokine data shown in Figure 2C

claim: In Adult Naive mice, a gradual increase of IL-6, CXCL1, and CCL2 was observed from 6 hpi to 24 hpi.
source: In Adult Naive mice, a gradual increase of these cytokines was observed from 6 hpi to 24 hpi (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by cytokine data shown in Figure 2C

claim: A prior UTI in C3H/HeN mice confers the ability to mount a robust early phase (first 6 hpi) inflammatory response to UPEC infection not seen in Adult Naive mice.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that a prior UTI in C3H/HeN mice confers the ability to mount a robust early phase (first 6 hpi) inflammatory response to UPEC infection not seen in Adult Naive mice, and that this inflammation is more likely to be sustained in Sensitized mice.
evidence: Inferred from the combined histopathology, bacterial burden, bladder weight, and cytokine data

claim: Early phase inflammation in response to UPEC infection is more likely to be sustained in Sensitized mice.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that a prior UTI in C3H/HeN mice confers the ability to mount a robust early phase (first 6 hpi) inflammatory response to UPEC infection not seen in Adult Naive mice, and that this inflammation is more likely to be sustained in Sensitized mice.
evidence: Inferred from the combined histopathology, bacterial burden, bladder weight, and cytokine data

claim: In Adult Naive mice, the number of differentially expressed genes increased with time, starting low at 3.5 hpi (291 genes), increasing by 6 hpi (5309 genes), and peaking at 24 hpi (9249 genes).
source: In Adult Naive mice, the number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) increased with time, starting low (291 genes at 3.5 hpi), increasing somewhat by 6 hpi (5309 genes), and peaking at 24 hpi (9249 genes).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A-B

claim: In Resolved mice, the number of differentially expressed genes was relatively low at 3.5 hpi (127 genes), peaked at 6 hpi (10872 genes), and decreased somewhat by 24 hpi (7793 genes).
source: However, in both Resolved and Sensitized mice, the number of DEGs was relatively low at 3.5 hpi (127 and 944 genes, respectively), but peaked at 6 hpi (10872 and 10133 genes, respectively), and decreased somewhat by 24 hpi (7793 and 8252 genes, respectively; Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A-B

claim: In Sensitized mice, the number of differentially expressed genes was relatively low at 3.5 hpi (944 genes), peaked at 6 hpi (10133 genes), and decreased somewhat by 24 hpi (8252 genes).
source: However, in both Resolved and Sensitized mice, the number of DEGs was relatively low at 3.5 hpi (127 and 944 genes, respectively), but peaked at 6 hpi (10872 and 10133 genes, respectively), and decreased somewhat by 24 hpi (7793 and 8252 genes, respectively; Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A-B

claim: Mock-infected Resolved mice were similar to Adult Naive mice in principal component analysis.
source: The PCA plot of the mock-infected mice demonstrated that Resolved mice were similar to Adult Naive mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by PCA data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Mock-infected Sensitized mice clustered separately from Resolved and Adult Naive mice in principal component analysis.

claim: The number of genes that were differentially expressed between the mock-infected Sensitized vs. Resolved groups (1019 genes) was similar to the number found in a previous study (992 genes).

evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to O'Brien et al., 2016

claim: 357 of the differentially expressed genes and 98 of the 139 enriched pathways were the same between the current study and a previous study comparing Sensitized vs. Resolved mice.

claim: Mice infected for 6 or 24 hr clustered separately from mice infected for 3.5 hr or mock-infected on the PC1 axis, regardless of infection history.

claim: Clustering of mice infected for 6 or 24 hr separately from mice infected for 3.5 hr or mock-infected is likely driven by infiltration of immune cells into the bladder tissue between 3.5 and 6 hpi in all mice.
source: This clustering is likely driven by infiltration of immune cells into the bladder tissue between 3.5 and 6 hpi in all mice.

claim: Sensitized mice clustered separately from Resolved and Adult Naive mice on the PC2 axis, irrespective of time point.
source: In contrast, Sensitized mice clustered separately from Resolved and Adult Naive mice on the PC2 axis, irrespective of time point (Figure 3D).

claim: In all mouse groups (Adult Naive, Resolved, and Sensitized) across all time points of infection, 13 or more of the top 20 most enriched pathways were directly related to inflammation and immunity.
source: Pathway analysis of the biological processes represented by the DEGs showed that in all mouse groups (Adult Naive, Resolved, and Sensitized) across all time points of infection, 13 or more of the top 20 most pathways enriched in UPEC-infected versus mock-infected bladders were directly related to inflammation and immunity, including immune cell development and recruitment, cytokine expression and pattern recognition receptor signaling (Supplementary file 1).

claim: TNFα receptor 1 (TNFR1) and TNFα receptor 2 (TNFR2) signaling pathways were among the most highly upregulated pathways during at least one time point for each mouse group.
source: TNFɑ receptor 1 (TNFR1) and TNFɑ receptor 2 (TNFR2) signaling pathways were among the most highly upregulated pathways as determined by z-score during at least one time point for each mouse group (Supplementary files 1 and 2).

claim: TNFα has been shown to be upregulated in C57BL/6 and CBA mice two hours after bladder infection.
source: Notably, TNFɑ has been shown to be upregulated in C57BL/6 and CBA mice two hours after bladder infection (Chan et al., 2013; Duell et al., 2012), demonstrating that this response is not unique to C3H/HeN mice.

claim: All mock-infected mice (whether Adult Naive, Resolved, or Sensitized) clustered together in hierarchical clustering of TNFα signaling pathway genes.

claim: At 24 hpi, strong TNFα signaling was present in 4 of 6 UPEC-infected Sensitized mice, but not in any Adult Naive or Resolved mice.

claim: The median bladder titer in Sensitized mice decreased from 3.8 × 10^6 cfu/bladder in isotype-treated mice to 8.4 × 10^3 cfu/bladder in TNFα-depleted mice at 24 hpi.

evidence: Supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 7A

claim: The nature of an initial mucosal infection can affect susceptibility to recurrent infection.
source: In immunocompetent individuals, an initial infectious disease episode—particularly one that can lead to chronic inflammation, such as upper respiratory infections (sinusitis, tonsillitis, and nasopharyngitis) and urinary tract infections—can act as a potent effector of tissue remodeling that predisposes to recurrent infection (Hooton et al., 1996; Nuhoglu et al., 2003; Toews, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hooton et al., 1996; Nuhoglu et al., 2003; Toews, 2005

claim: The character of a prior bladder infection can alter the kinetics and downstream effects of disease checkpoints.
source: Based on our prior investigations of this model (Hannan et al., 2010; Hannan et al., 2014; O'Brien et al., 2016; Schwartz et al., 2015; O'Brien et al., 2018), we hypothesized that early host-pathogen interactions at the bladder mucosa trigger time-sensitive checkpoints that determine the outcome of infection, but that the character of a prior bladder infection can alter the kinetics and downstream effects of these disease checkpoints.
evidence: Hypothesis based on prior work cited

claim: TNFα plays a role in the bladder's response to UPEC infection in naive mice.

claim: Both the kinetics and the effects of TNFα response can vary substantially based upon host infection history.

claim: TNFα binds to TNFR1 and/or TNFR2 and can activate distinct signaling cascades based on the receptors it binds to and the local microenvironment.
source: TNFɑ binds to TNFR1 (expressed in most tissues, including urothelial cells) and/or TNFR2 (typically expressed by immune cells) and can activate distinct signaling cascades based on the receptors it binds to and the local microenvironment (Wajant et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2018; Wang and Bjorling, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wajant et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2018; Wang and Bjorling, 2011

claim: Both forms of TNFα can activate TNFR1, which leads either to NF-κB activation, cell survival, and cytokine production or cell death by apoptosis or necroptosis.

evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018

claim: Only membrane-bound TNFα can activate TNFR2, thereby stimulating cell-mediated immunity.

evidence: Inferred from pathway analysis results and known biology of TNFR signaling
